findings.title: Every v9 answer counted right on the test set reads the right entity; the ticket_link ones rely on the 50-document bank boundary
findings.evidence: I inspected each of the 48 fully right v9 answers with planner.ends and field values. The plans fit the questions: compare starts from exactly the two named tickets with both due dates read; person plans are person → assignee_of [linear]; action items are item → owner → assignee_of [linear]; issue_pr_author is key → referenced_by [github] → author; pr_issue is PR → linked_linear [linear] → field with a single end. There are no hub-cluster or other-ticket coincidences. All 6 right ticket_link answers follow 'dependencies' to 2-4 tickets, e.g. ENG-4862 → ENG-4822/4823/4827/4829. Only the gold ticket is a document in the bank; the others are bare identifiers with no fields, so 'single' returns the gold value. Those tickets do exist as documents in the full benchmark (ENG-4822, ENG-4827, ENG-421007 and ENG-60123 each have several). rests_on passes because the gold key is among the ends. The one wrong link answer (ticket_link-status-039) needs 'parent_issue'. v9's 66 training ticket_link questions used only 'dependencies' or 'linked_issues', and 6 of the 7 test ticket_links are 'dependencies'. The half-right action_owner_issues-021 (F1 0.5) chose due_date → earliest, plausibly because of the word 'date' inside the quoted action-item text.
findings.impact: 'Right for the right reason' at 0.968 is genuine on this bank. The ticket_link part reflects the small-bank construction: the plan never singles out 'the other ticket', and in a larger bank the same plan would return nothing or a mixed value. Link generalisation beyond the 'dependencies' relation is untested.

findings.title: The changed-information copy changes only 13 of 50 expected answers
findings.evidence: Between mdplan and mdplanchanged, 37 of 50 expected answers are identical: keys, counts and statuses are unchanged, and the 23-day date shift keeps every comparison order. Only person names (authors and assignees) and 3 due dates change. v9 gives the renamed or shifted value on all 13. Every arm, v4 and v8 included, scores identically on both copies.
findings.impact: Rule 6 is met correctly, but identical scores are largely expected by construction. It shows the plans do not memorise names or dates; it does not show robustness to changed statuses, links or counts.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute any number in the finding. Comparing mdplan/questions.jsonl with mdplanchanged/questions.jsonl: the same 50 ids, and 37 expected answers are identical. 13 change: 10 person names (5 issue_pr_author authors, 2 pr_issue assignees, 3 ticket_link assignees) and 3 pr_issue due dates (023 and 033 move from 2026-02-14 to 2026-03-09; 034 moves from 2025-02-28 to 2025-03-23).

This follows from how the copy is built. factbank_split.changed only renames every person and moves every ISO date 23 days later (SHIFT_DAYS=23). The legacy option that also renamed statuses was not used. Keys, statuses, links and counts are therefore unchanged. Because every date moves by the same amount, every earlier/later order is kept.

In plan_report.json, v9 and v10 give the renamed or shifted value on all 13 changed rows, scoring 1.0 on each. Per question, the direct and reason scores are identical across the two copies for every arm (v1, v4, v8, v9, v9n, v10): 0 rows differ. v4 and v8 are also right on the same few changed rows on both copies, for example pr_issue-assignee-027 and 029.

Two corrections to the finding's wording:
(a) "Every arm scores identically" holds for the scored metrics (direct and reason) but not for the secondary pieces-coverage metric. v4's 24000 mean is 0.982 on the test set and 0.959 on the changed copy. v1's 2000 mean is 0.645 against 0.650, and its 24000 mean 0.996 against 1.000. These come from 7 person questions.
(b) "Largely expected by construction" overstates the point. Of the 37 unchanged answers, only 6 involve nothing that changed: the status questions pr_issue-status-016/019 and ticket_link-status-020/025/026/039. The other 31 still name a renamed person in the question (15) or pass through renamed people or shifted dates on the way to the answer (23; the two groups overlap). So the copy does test that plans and banks do not depend on remembered names or dates. It does not test changes to statuses, links, counts or date order.
verdict.corrected: Where rule 6 is reported, the write-up should say: "The changed copy is made by a fixed transform that renames every person and moves every ISO date 23 days later. Keys, statuses, links and counts stay the same, and so does the order of any two dates. As a result, 13 of the 50 expected answers change (10 person names and 3 due dates) and 37 stay the same. Of those 37, 31 still name a renamed person in the question (15) or reach the answer through renamed people or shifted dates (23; the two overlap). Only 6 status questions are untouched. v9 and v10 give the new value on all 13 changed answers. Every arm, v4 and v8 included, has the same per-question direct and right-for-the-right-reason scores on both copies. Only the secondary retrieval-coverage figures move slightly for v1 and v4 (v4 at 24000: 0.982 against 0.959). Rule 6 therefore shows that the plans do not depend on remembered names or dates. It does not test robustness to changed statuses, links, counts or date order, so identical scores on the changed copy are weak evidence beyond that."

(2) Probe. lens_review/probes/w3 holds the test's 50 questions with writer 3's wordings. Its questions match the main session's mdplan_w3 byte for byte. The "same" control probe reproduces the official numbers exactly: v9 0.975, misses -021 and ticket_link-status-039. - mdwords: 0.473
- mdblind: 0.412

- mdplan: 0.323

- There are 60 word types.
- 26 of them are unseen in the training wordings.
- Only 6 are unseen across training plus all wordings of the five earlier sets: confirm, gimme, provide, refs, respond, titl. That is 3.5% of tokens (6 of 170).

| set | share |
|---|---|
| mdtest | 0.322 |
| mdfresh | 0.316 |
| mdwords | 0.476 |
| mdblind | 0.421 |
| mdllm | 0.410 |
| mdplan | 0.335 |

- pr_issue/due_date: 0/3
- person_first: 2/7
- action_owner_issues: 0.38

verdict.reason:
The finding's main claim holds, but the reason it gives is wrong. All the numbers it cites reproduce:
- v4 scores 0.510, below every earlier set (0.586 to 0.727, mean 0.635).
- In the training wordings v4 scores 0.573 (lens_review/probes/train).
- By kind: issue_pr_author 0/5, pr_issue/due_date 0/3, person_first 2/7, action_owner_issues 0.375.
- Across the six sets, r(v4, v9) = -0.12.
- v9 - v4 is +0.465 here, against +0.231 to +0.397 on the earlier sets (mean 0.322).
- The smallest probe margin is about 0.309 (the blind probe: 0.940 - 0.632).

**The test documents are hard for v4, and the wording is not.**
- With the wording held fixed, v4 scores lower on these 50 questions than on the earlier set that used the same wording:
  - BLIND: 0.632 against 0.727;
  - NEW_WORDS: 0.416 against 0.611;
  - BLIND2: 0.488 against 0.586.
- v9 does not drop the same way (0.940 against 0.958, 0.923 against 0.877, 0.940 against 0.983).
- With the documents held fixed, the drawn wording is about average for v4: 0.510, against a mean of 0.515 over six other blind wordings of the same questions (0.416 to 0.632).

1. "Rule 1's margin is partly due to the mix of kinds." The kind mix is ordinary. Every set has nearly the same make-up; this one has 5 issue_pr_author and 3 pr_issue/due_date questions, about as many as the earlier sets. Applying v4's per-kind rates, pooled from the five earlier sets, to each set's own mix predicts:
   - 0.623 for the test;
   - 0.614 to 0.654 for the earlier sets.

2. "Its losses come from kinds it never learned." Only pr_issue/due_date is missing from v4's 48 training questions (mdtrain).
   - person_first was learned: v4 got 7/7 in training, 7/7 on these same test questions in the training wordings, and 7/7 on the BLIND and BLIND2 probes. Its 2/7 is caused by the drawn wording.
   - person_count is also a wording loss: 8/8 in the training wordings, 4/8 as drawn.
   - action_owner_issues was learned (0.88 in training). Here it scores 0.61 even in the training wordings, which points to the documents.

1. v9 and v9n answered "ENG-4822", a ticket key and not a status. That is not the status under either reading, so ambiguity is not what produced the recorded miss.
2. The cause is the blind wording "where that other ticket currently stands". The test set used it on this one question only. Applied to the other six link tickets in the bank, v9 returns no status for any of them:

findings.title: The changed copy's identical scores are expected by construction
findings.evidence: mdplanchanged keeps the same wordings. 15 questions differ only in renamed people, and 13 expected answers change. Plan shapes are identical between the two copies for 50/50 questions with v8, v9 and v10, and 49/50 with v4. The runs are genuinely separate: the 'all pieces within 24,000 chars' figure for v4 differs, 0.982 against 0.959.
findings.impact: Rule 6 checks only robustness to renamed people and shifted dates, not wording. The identical scores are no sign of a copying error, but they add no evidence about generalisation.

verdict.reason:
I checked every factual claim in the finding against the data and all of them hold. The write-up already makes the main point, though.

- **Wordings:** In mdplan and mdplanchanged/questions.jsonl, all 50 ids match. Only 15 question texts differ (person_count-001..014 and person_first-002..015), and the only change is a renamed person, such as Ravi Desai becoming Quilla Varga. The other 35 wordings are identical.
- **Answers:** 13 expected answers change: 6 author, 6 assignee and 3 due dates moved 23 days later. Gold documents are the same in all 50.
- **Plan shapes:** I dropped the renamed start entity from each `reason` and compared what was left. The shapes are identical in 50/50 for v8, v9, v9n and v10, and 49/50 for v4; the exception is person_first-004, which takes a different route.
- **Answers across copies:** Applying the rename map from renamed.json plus the 23-day shift to the mdplan answers reproduces the mdplanchanged answers exactly for v8, v9, v9n and v10. For v4 it does so for 49/50, the exception again being person_first-004.
- **Separate runs:** The runs really were separate. The report gives v4 "all pieces within 24,000 chars" as 0.982 on the test set and 0.959 on the changed copy.

So the identical scores come from the transform (factbank_split changed renames people and moves dates). They are not a copying error, and rule 6 does not test wording at all.

However, FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS.md lines 91-95 already say: "People are renamed and dates shifted, which changes 13 expected answers. Every arm scores exactly as on the original. That is expected... It shows nothing about changed statuses, links or counts."

What the write-up leaves out is that the changed copy also keeps the test set's wordings, so rule 6 says nothing about wording either. That is a small clarification. It does not change any rule verdict or headline number.
verdict.corrected: Optional clarification under "The changed copy" in FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS.md: "The copy keeps the test set's wordings. Only 15 questions change, and only by a renamed person; gold documents are unchanged. Plans have the same shape on both copies (50/50 for v8, v9, v9n and v10; 49/50 for v4). So rule 6 checks only that renamed people and dates moved 23 days do not break the plans. It says nothing about new wordings or about changed statuses, links or counts."

findings.title: Rule 4 could not be met on this test set, and v9, v9n and v10 behaved as one arm
findings.evidence: Once v9 scored 0.975 on mdplan, v10 could reach at most 1.0, so v10 − v9 could be at most 0.025, below the 0.05 threshold. The factbank_v10.jsonl rows show the bank's learned kind was sure (floor 0.9) on 49 of 50 questions. On all 49 the form's kind matched the learned kind, so the form was used on one question only: ticket_link-status-039, 'Ticket ENG-4823 is linked to another ticket…', expected 'In Review'. There it changed the plan (v9 answered 'ENG-4822'; v10 followed 'referenced_by → status' and answered 'Done'), and both answers are wrong. The same holds on the changed copy. v9 and v9n gave identical answers and plans on all 50 test questions, so the glossary changed nothing either. On the earlier sets the form could act more often: the learned kind was unsure 13/50 times on mdfresh and 27/50 on mdwords.
findings.impact: 'Rule 4 not met' is not evidence that the form adds nothing. On this set the test had no power: the form was consulted once and the ceiling ruled the rule out. Likewise v9n = v9 here says nothing about the glossary. The write-up should report v10 and v9n as untested by this set, not as no better. The pre-registration warned about this ceiling, and the numbers confirm it.

verdict.reason:
I re-checked the data read-only and the finding's main claims hold.

1. **The ceiling.** v9 scored 0.975 on mdplan (link 0.947, combine 0.978, compare 1.000). The most v10 can score is 1.0, so v10 − v9 can be at most 0.025, which is below the 0.05 the rule needs. The pre-registration warned of this: "rule 4 can only be met if the new wordings leave v9 more room."

2. **v9 and v9n.** In mdplan and mdplanchanged, factbank_v9.jsonl and factbank_v9n.jsonl give the same (answer, reason) pair on all 50 questions.

3. **v10 against v9.** v10 differs from v9 on exactly one question, ticket_link-status-039, in both copies. The expected answer is 'In Review'.
   - v9's plan goes title → referenced_by → dependencies → dependencies and answers 'ENG-4822'.
   - v10's plan goes title → referenced_by → status and answers 'Done'.
   - Both answers are wrong.

4. **The learned kind.** form.learned_kind is None on 1 of 50 rows, so the floor was met on 49. On all 49 the form's kind equals the learned kind.

5. **The earlier sets.** The learned kind was unsure on 13 of 50 questions in mdfresh and 27 of 50 in mdwords. Both counts match the finding.

**One part of the finding is wrong.** It says "the form was used on one question only". The code does more than that. In `plans.answer` the form's fields are passed to check 5 whenever the form's kind equals the kind being used, and that includes the 49 questions where the lessons were sure.
- 37 of those 49 forms carried fields.
- About 30 of them are kinds where check 5 can bind: person, date, other, or a key chosen by a due date.
- The check changed no answer there.
- `Former.form` called the model on every question: every row has a model_ms of about 1.6–1.9 s, and the first has 20.7 s.

So the accurate statement is: the form decided the kind once, its field check ran on most questions, and the outcome changed on one.

**The published write-up already covers most of this.** FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS.md, review items 3 and 4, says that "not met" means this test could not show it, and that v9 = v9n = v10 is a product of the draw. Two passages still conflict with the data and with those items:
- "so the model was asked once" in the summary, and the v10 table row "unsure ... so the form was used: 1 of 50". The doc's own timing row reports the model's time per question.
- Under "What this shows": "No language model is needed for this when the wording is ordinary. v9n ... matches v9 on the test." This cites as evidence the very equality that review item 4 calls uninformative.

The rule-4 verdict and the scores are unaffected.

Keep "Rule 4: not met (0.975 against 0.975)" and add: "Once v9 scored 0.975, v10 could gain at most +0.025, so rule 4 could not be met on this draw. The pre-registration foresaw this ceiling. The test therefore says nothing about whether the form adds; v10 and v9n are untested by this set, not shown to be no better."

Replace "so the model was asked once" and the table row "questions where the bank's own lessons were unsure of the kind of answer, so the form was used | 1 of 50" with these three rows:
- "The model filled in a form for all 50 questions."
- "Its kind was used on 1 (the lessons were sure on 49, and the form's kind agreed with theirs on all 49). Its field check (check 5) also ran on the questions where its kind agreed."
- "Its answer differed from v9's on 1 question only (ticket_link-status-039: v9 'ENG-4822', v10 'Done', expected 'In Review'; both wrong). The same holds on the changed copy."

Add: "v9 and v9n gave identical answers and plans on all 50 test questions (and on the changed copy), so the glossary was not exercised by this draw."

In "What this shows", drop "v9n, with no model anywhere, matches v9 on the test" as support for "no language model is needed". If the claim stays, base it only on the single-wording runs (writer 2: v9n = v9 = 0.975). State that on writers 1 and 3 the glossary added +0.035 and +0.029.

findings.title: The blind wordings came from the same writer brief as two development sets, so the test vocabulary was almost all seen in development
findings.evidence: The session transcript shows the writers' brief (14:47:19) is word for word the KINDS brief used for the mdblind (2026-10-08 00:44) and mdllm (03:52) wordings. Both of those sets were then used to develop v9 and v10. The brief itself uses the training vocabulary: 'assigned to', 'due', 'status', 'linked to another ticket', 'opened (authored)', and suggests '#{n}'/'PR #{n}'/'pull request #{n}'. Of the 91 distinct words in the 20 selected test wordings, 38 are absent from the training wordings. Only 7 are absent from all wordings used in development (T held-out, RETEST, NEW_WORDS, BLIND, BLIND2), and most of those are filler: confirm, gimme, provide, refs, respond, state's, titled. The draw also used only 3 of the 6 pr_issue wordings: assignee only writer 1, and due_date and status only writer 2. The personas are new, the writers worked independently, and the selection rule was applied as stated, so this is not a departure.
findings.impact: The 0.975 measures new documents with wordings close to the development distribution, not robustness to unseen phrasing. The jump from v4 0.510 to v9 0.975 partly reflects that development tuned the planner on wordings from the same brief. Generalisation claims should be worded to match.

I checked the finding against the data, read-only, and its facts hold. Its impact statement goes further than the data supports, and the write-up already states most of its consequence.

   - 38 absent from the training wordings (T[0]);

- **The robustness point is already stated.** The write-up at HEAD (a58ca03) says:

  - the test used 17 of 20 wordings;
  - review item 5: of 60 content-word types only 6 had not appeared in training or any development wording, and this makes it "a weaker test of unfamiliar wording than the new-words set".

**What is missing.** Neither the pre-registration nor the write-up says that the writers got the same task description as the earlier blind sets' writers. That description itself uses the training phrasing, which explains the overlap. It is a one-sentence disclosure. It changes no number or rule verdict.

Add one sentence to review item 5 ("The test's words were not very new"), for example:

"One reason is the writers' brief. Each writer got the same description of what each question must ask as the language-model test's writers: the general-English blind set used the same one with three small differences. findings.title: The changed copy keeps every key, link, status and date order, so identical scores are expected by construction
findings.evidence: The mdplanchanged log shows 93 people renamed and a +23-day shift, legacy=false. Comparing the two questions.jsonl files: 15 questions change wording (all person_count and person_first, through the renamed names), and only 13 of 50 expected answers change (5 PR authors, 2 PR-issue assignees, 3 ticket assignees, 3 due dates). The other 37 are byte-identical: keys, counts and statuses, plus compare and first-due answers, because a uniform date shift keeps the order. The changed bank was rebuilt from erb_changed and its answers carry the new names. No original full name is left in the changed documents or questions. Every arm picks the same plan on all 50 questions (the plan text differs on 15 only through renamed names) and gets identical per-question scores and right-for-the-right-reason flags. The v10 forms and learned kinds are identical across copies. Two gaps in the transform: shift_dates' trailing \b fails before 'T', so timestamps such as fireflies recorded_at ('2025-11-19T15:00:00Z') and incident_timeline are not shifted; and bare first names stay ('Jordan' 73 times, 'Priya' 66, 'Maya' 61). No question reads either. One useful side check: the learned-kind naive Bayes vocabulary contains training person-name tokens (priya, nair, lee, ravi, kim…), and 'Priya Nair' appears in both training and test questions. Renaming her left every learned kind unchanged, so those tokens did not help.
findings.impact: Rule 6 being met shows that renamed people are still recognised and that the bank re-reads values. It is not evidence of robustness to changed structure. Any arm that does not memorise specific names or dates passes it. The equal scores across all arms are what the transform guarantees, not a separate finding.

verdict.reason:
I checked the data read-only and almost every factual claim holds. One is wrong, and the main point is already in the published write-up.

Confirmed:
- run_test.log shows 93 people renamed, a 23-day shift and legacy=false.
- 15 questions change wording, all of them person_count (8) or person_first (7).
- 13 expected answers change: 5 issue_pr_author names, 2 pr_issue assignee names, 3 pr_issue due dates and 3 ticket_link names. The other 37 are identical: keys, counts, statuses, and the compare and first-due keys.
- No renamed full name is left in erb_changed or in the changed questions.
- For v8, v9, v9n and v10, the plan text and answers on the changed copy are exactly the originals with names renamed and dates shifted. Per-question own scores and right-for-the-right-reason flags are identical for all five arms.
- v10 forms and learned_kind are identical apart from model_ms.
- The shift_dates `\b...\b` pattern skips dates followed by 'T'. All 16 timestamps in the documents are left unshifted (recorded_at 7, incident_timeline, follow_up_meeting and others).
- Bare first names stay: Jordan 73, Priya 66, Maya 61, Alex 38.
- No question piece, question or v9 read touches a timestamp or a bare first name.
- The plan_lessons_v9 vocabularies (rel/agg/kind_assoc, asked_kind) contain priya, nair, ravi, kim and lee. 'Priya Nair' appears 21 times in the training questions and twice in the test questions.

Refuted: "every arm picks the same plan on all 50 questions" is false for v4. On person_first-004, v4 starts from an action item before the change and from a PR after it, answering 'Ethan Cole' and then 'Pascoe Abernathy' (not the rename of Ethan Cole, who became Mireille Strand). Both answers are wrong, so the score does not change. Equal scores are therefore not guaranteed by the transform for an arm that depends on names; they are only expected for arms that read names and dates rather than remember them.

Already in the write-up: since a58ca03, docs/FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS.md (the changed-copy section, from line 93) says that keys, statuses, links, counts and date order stay the same, that 15 questions and 13 answers change, that equal scores are expected, and that the copy "shows nothing about new wordings, or about changed statuses, links or counts". The impact is already stated.

What is not stated: the write-up says the transform "renames every person and moves every date 23 days later". That overstates it, given the unshifted timestamps and the bare first names left in. No score or rule verdict changes.
verdict.corrected:
Replace the first bullet of "The changed copy" in docs/FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS.md, and add one bullet, as follows:
- "The fixed transform renames every person's full name (93 people) and moves every plain ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD) 23 days later. Two gaps: the 16 timestamps written with a time (e.g. Fireflies recorded_at '2025-11-19T15:00:00Z', incident_timeline) are not moved, because the date pattern needs a word boundary and 'T' follows the date; and bare first names ('Jordan' 73 times, 'Priya' 66, 'Maya' 61) are kept. No test question reads either. Keys, statuses, links and counts stay the same, and so does the order of any two plain dates."
- After "Every arm scores exactly as on the original": "with the same right-for-the-right-reason flags. v8, v9, v9n and v10 pick the same plan on all 50 questions (on 15 the text differs only by the renamed names), and v10's forms are unchanged. v4 picked a different plan on one question (person_first-004), wrong both times. So rule 6 shows that renamed people are recognised and values re-read; it is not a test of robustness to changed structure."

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute the finding with read-only checks and could not. Every claim held:

(1) Form files. scratchpad/plan9/forms/form_mdplan.jsonl and form_mdplanchanged.jsonl each have 50 lines. Each line is a different question, and the lines run in the same order as that folder's questions.jsonl. Every line has prompt bf3f84a670bd43be and model llama3.2:3b.

(2) Timings. Test set: first call 20662.8 ms, median 1861.3 ms, total 113.06 s. Changed copy: first call 2345.3 ms, longest 2743.2 ms, median 1863.75 ms, total 96.09 s.

(3) The files were new and written during the run. stat gives the creation time of form_mdplan.jsonl as 16:45:26.28. That is about 20.8 s after factbank_v9n.jsonl was last written (16:45:05.44), which matches the 20.7 s first call followed by the first append. Its last write was 16:47:07.64, and factbank_v10.jsonl was last written at 16:47:07.86. form_mdplanchanged.jsonl was created at 16:47:51.90, just after v9n finished at 16:47:49.37; it was last written at 16:49:34.86, and v10 finished at 16:49:35.05. So neither file existed before its v10 step. Former only reads its own cache file and calls Ollama when a question is missing, so with an empty cache every form came from the model.

(4) The answers used those forms. In both folders, all 50 v10 rows carry a form whose raw output and model_ms match the cache line exactly (0 mismatches).

(5) No earlier cache held these questions. None of the form caches written before 16:44 (mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdllm, mdtrain, mdtrainall, mdtrainv9) contains any test question. The w1 and w2 caches do share some test questions (22 and 28), but they were written at 17:38 and later, for the blind-wording probe after the run.

(6) The model settings and prompt match the pre-registration. Former._ask sends temperature 0, seed 0 and num_predict 60, which matches the pre-registration (temperature 0, seed 0, at most 60 tokens). reader.py at HEAD is identical to reader.py at the freeze commit 7017046. form_fingerprint() returns bf3f84a670bd43be.

(7) The repo copies match. The files in cie/docs/benchmarks/factbank_plan/forms have the same sha256 as the scratchpad files for both test caches and the others I checked.

(8) The write-up agrees. FACTBANK_PLAN_RESULTS.md reports mean 2.3 s, median 1.9 s and at most 21 s. The data give mean 2.26 s, median 1.86 s and at most 20.66 s.

So v10 was run as pre-registered, and v10 = v9 is not caused by stale or reused forms. The finding confirms the published results, and the write-up needs no correction.
verdict.corrected: No correction is needed. Optionally, the v10 section could add one sentence: "The test-set and changed-copy form caches were created during the run itself (form_mdplan.jsonl created at 16:45:26, after v9n finished at 16:45:05; form_mdplanchanged.jsonl created at 16:47:52).
